A study of Spoofer Project measurements for the year ending 2019-08-01 found that outbound source address validation (SAV) was not universal. At least one prefix lacked outbound spoofed-packet filtering in 25.2% of tested IPv4 autonomous systems (ASes) and 32.1% of tested IPv6 ASes. Among tested prefixes, 14.9% of IPv4 prefixes without NAT and 12.3% of IPv6 prefixes did not filter outbound spoofed packets; 6.4% of IPv4 prefixes tested behind NAT did not filter them.

In Spoofer Project measurements for the year ending 2019-08-01, inbound filtering of packets claiming to originate within the client’s own subnet was less widely deployed than outbound filtering: 67.0% of tested IPv4 ASes and 74.2% of tested IPv6 ASes had at least one prefix that did not filter such inbound packets.

A comparison of IPv4 tests from networks without NAT found no general improvement in outbound spoofed-source filtering between 2006-05-01..2006-05-07 and the year ending 2019-08-01. In May 2006, 18.3% of tested IPv4/24 prefixes and 20.4% of tested ASes did not block spoofed-source packets; for the later period, the corresponding figures were 14.9% of prefixes and 30.5% of ASes.

Analysis of Spoofer tests collected from 2016-05 through 2019-08 found no meaningful correlation between the age of an IPv4 prefix in the global BGP routing table and the probability that a client in that prefix could send spoofed packets. Prefix age was measured from its first appearance in monthly Routeviews and RIPE RIS snapshots; Pearson correlation showed no meaningful relationship.

The Spoofer study identifies crowd-sourced measurement limitations: opt-in participation may create sample bias; results are unevenly distributed across time and networks; Internet equipment, configuration, and policies change; and one test may not represent a whole network, prefix, or AS. Sparse observations also make it difficult to infer whether a network remediated a filtering problem.

The daemonized Spoofer client ran measurements when it detected a newly attached network and repeated tests weekly on previously seen networks. Even so, between 2016-05 and 2019-08, 44% of IPv4 /24 prefixes and 32% of ASes reported measurements in only one week; only 8% of IPv4 /24 prefixes and 23% of ASes reported measurements in at least 20 weeks. AT&T, Comcast, Verizon, Deutsche Telekom, Charter, and Cox had measurements in nearly every week after the daemonized client’s release.

A chronological per-prefix model trained on earlier Spoofer measurements achieved over 90% accuracy across IP versions and source-address classes, though the study cautioned that accuracy was a poor metric because spoofability was uncommon. By August 2019, recall exceeded 80% for IPv6 and was about 50–70% for IPv4; IPv6 predictions outperformed IPv4 in precision as well. The model’s poor precision for IPv4 private addresses was attributed to filtering in the network core obscuring edge-network policies.

For the year ending 2019-08-01, Spoofer received IPv4 reports from 2,783 ASes, of which 2,418 (86.8%) had tests involving a NAT. NATs rewrite source addresses so hosts with private IPv4 addresses can communicate externally, but NAT use does not guarantee spoofed packets are blocked: 6.4% of tested IPv4 /24 prefixes behind NAT did not filter spoofed-source packets. The study also notes that NAT is rare in IPv6, where SAV is needed explicitly; 12.3% of tested IPv6 /40 prefixes did not filter outbound spoofed packets.

The paper describes two ways a NAT may fail to block spoofed packets: it may forward the packet with the spoofed source address intact, or it may rewrite the source address to the NAT’s publicly routable address. The supplied excerpt ends before the second failure mode is fully explained.
